title: Subarray With Elements Greater Than Varying Threshold
description:
You are given an integer array `nums` and an integer `threshold`.

A non-empty contiguous subarray of length `L` is **valid** when every element in it is strictly greater than `threshold / L` (real division, not integer division).

Return the **smallest** length `L` of any valid subarray. If no valid subarray exists, return `-1`.

**Example 1:**
```
Input: nums = [1,3,4,3,1], threshold = 6
Output: 3
Explanation: For length 3 every element must exceed 6 / 3 = 2, and [3,4,3] works. Length 1 needs an element above 6 and length 2 needs two adjacent elements above 3, neither of which exists.
```

**Example 2:**
```
Input: nums = [6,5,6,5,8], threshold = 7
Output: 1
Explanation: The single element 8 is greater than 7 / 1 = 7, so length 1 already works and it is the smallest possible.
```

**Example 3:**
```
Input: nums = [1,1,1], threshold = 10
Output: -1
Explanation: Even the whole array (length 3) would need every element above 10 / 3, so no valid subarray exists.
```

examples.explanation: For length 3 every element must exceed 6 / 3 = 2, and [3,4,3] works. Length 1 needs an element above 6 and length 2 needs two adjacent elements above 3, neither of which exists.
The single element 8 is greater than 7 / 1 = 7, so length 1 already works and it is the smallest possible.
Even the whole array (length 3) would need every element above 10 / 3, so no valid subarray exists.

solution_approach: A brute force tries every subarray and checks min * L > threshold, which is O(n^2) even with a running minimum. The condition only depends on the subarray minimum m and its length L: it holds exactly when m * L > threshold. For each index i treated as the minimum, a monotonic stack gives the nearest strictly smaller element on each side, so the widest window where nums[i] is the minimum has length W_i. Every length from 1 to W_i is achievable with nums[i] as a lower bound on the minimum, so index i certifies all lengths L in [floor(threshold / nums[i]) + 1, W_i]. The smallest valid length is therefore the minimum over i of floor(threshold / nums[i]) + 1, taken only where that value is <= W_i; if no index qualifies, return -1. This uses O(n) time and O(n) space.
hints: Every element of the subarray exceeding threshold / L is the same as saying the subarray minimum times L is greater than threshold.
For each element, find how far the window can stretch left and right while that element stays the minimum. A monotonic stack gives these boundaries in linear time.
If nums[i] can be the minimum of a window of width up to W, the shortest length it can certify is floor(threshold / nums[i]) + 1. Take the smallest such length that does not exceed W.
follow_up_questions: How would you return the largest valid length instead of the smallest?
Can you solve it with a union-find approach that processes elements in decreasing order of value?
